To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) children who have a high level of dental fear are at increased risk of developing long-term dental anxiety and avoidance of dental care; (ii) the most common source of dental fear in children is previous negative dental experiences; (iii) the most common coping style in children is cognitive coping (e.g., thinking about the dental visit); (iv) the most common strategy used by children to cope with dental fear is distraction, followed by cognitive coping;
the effects of the intervention on child distress in dental settings were dependent upon the coping style of the child.
The effects of the intervention are not as strong as we expected, and the intervention did not have any effect on the children’s distress.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of coping styles in the management of children’s distress in the dental environment.
the effects of coping on children's distress during dental treatment.
the effects of preparatory interventions on children's distress and coping in the dental setting, and with the matching of interventions with coping style.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of the dental fear survey (DFS) is a reliable and valid instrument that can be used to assess fear of dentistry.
the effects of the intervention on children's distress were not significantly different for children with high and low levels of coping style.
a matching preparatory intervention to a coping style can be effective in reducing children's distress during a dental procedure.

children who are anxious about dental treatment can be successfully treated using a range of psychological interventions, including preparatory information, distraction, and relaxation training.
